8-1.question: An opponent discards {{east}} on their first turn. Which conclusions are reasonable?
options: They are unlikely to be collecting honour tiles
{{east}} is safe to discard against them for the rest of this rotation
They are definitely building a single-suit flush
They no longer hold any honour tiles
8-1.explanation: An early honour discard says little about suit shape, but it does mean they cannot use that honour against you this rotation.

8-1.question: An opponent throws {{s1}}, {{s5}} and {{s9}} in their first three turns but keeps every Dot tile. Which suit are they most likely collecting?
8-1.explanation: Throwing Bamboo at every rank early says Bamboo is not their suit, so the suit they never touch is the likely target.

8-1.question: Match each discard pattern to the most likely reading.

pairs.left: Throws {{p1}} and {{p9}} on turn 1
pairs.right: Circles terminals are not needed

pairs.left: Discards every Character drawn, turn after turn
pairs.right: Characters are not their suit

pairs.left: Throws honours on every early turn
pairs.right: Not collecting honour tiles

pairs.left: Suddenly stops discarding Bamboo
pairs.right: May have picked up Bamboo

8-1.explanation: Early discards reveal what a hand does not want, while a sudden change of pattern reveals what it has started to collect.

8-1.question: Four early discards from the same opponent are shown. Which one is the strongest evidence that they are avoiding the middle of that suit?
options: s5
east
p1
m9
8-1.explanation: A middle tile is the most useful tile in its suit, so throwing it early is the clearest sign the suit is unwanted.

8-1.question: An opponent who kept every honour tile for ten turns now discards {{south}}. What does this most likely mean?
options: They have given up on an honour-based plan
They are collecting honours harder than before
They have no hand at all
Their hand is already complete
8-1.explanation: A late honour discard usually means the honour plan was dropped once the hand took its real shape.

8-2.question: Which of these make a tile safer to discard?
options: All four copies are already visible on the table
The opponent you fear discarded it earlier this rotation
Nobody has discarded this tile yet
Two different opponents have already discarded it
8-2.explanation: Visible copies and discards by the players you fear both cut the chance that the tile completes their hand.

8-2.question: Match each situation to how safe that tile is against the player you fear.

pairs.left: They discarded it earlier this rotation
pairs.right: Absolutely safe against them until they draw

pairs.left: They discarded it, then drew twice
pairs.right: Only relatively safe

pairs.left: All four copies lie on the table
pairs.right: Cannot be won on at all

pairs.left: Never seen in the game, mid-hand
pairs.right: Most dangerous

8-2.explanation: Absolute safety lasts only until the opponent draws again, while four visible copies means no fifth copy exists to win on.

8-2.question: Why is a tile with all four copies visible completely safe to discard?
options: No opponent can hold or wait on a fifth copy
It must be an honour tile
Every player has already thrown it
It must be a terminal tile
8-2.explanation: There are only four copies of any tile, so once all four are visible nobody can complete a pair, pong or wait with it.

8-2.question: Which of these is NOT a reason for a tile to be safe?
options: The threatening opponent discarded it this rotation
All four copies are visible
It is a fresh middle tile nobody has played
Two opponents have already thrown it away
8-2.explanation: A fresh middle tile is the classic danger tile, because it connects to many sequences and all four copies are still live.

8-2.question: You can see all four copies of {{p6}} on the table. How many copies could an opponent still be waiting on?
8-2.explanation: All four copies are accounted for, so no opponent can be waiting on a tile that no longer exists in play.

8-3.question: Which situations call for folding rather than pushing?
options: Your hand is several tiles from ready and two opponents have called melds
You are comfortably leading and the hand is nearly over
You are one tile from a cheap win and nobody looks close
An opponent has three exposed melds and discards are getting dangerous
8-3.explanation: Folding pays when your own hand is far off or you have something to protect and someone else is close.

8-3.question: Match each table situation to the right response.

pairs.left: Four tiles from ready, opponent holds three melds
pairs.right: Fold and discard only safe tiles

pairs.left: One tile from a cheap win, nobody threatening
pairs.right: Push for the win

pairs.left: Leading late, your winning tile is dangerous
pairs.right: Hold the tile and take the draw

pairs.left: Far behind with five turns left
pairs.right: Push a bigger hand and accept risk

8-3.explanation: Defence is a choice about relative position, not a fixed rule, so the same hand can call for folding or pushing.

8-3.question: A player who folds scores nothing, but also pays nothing when the hand ends in a ___.
8-3.explanation: A drawn hand involves no payments at all, which is why folding can cost less than chasing a hopeless win.

8-3.question: Is it ever right to break up a meld you already hold just to find a safe discard?
options: Yes, when an opponent is clearly close and no safe tile is free
No, a meld must never be broken
Only on the first turn
Only if you are the dealer
8-3.explanation: When folding, the hand's value is already given up, so structure can be sacrificed to avoid dealing in.

8-3.question: You are far behind on points with ten tiles left in the wall and no opponent looks close. What is the best approach?
options: Push for a bigger hand and accept some risk
Fold immediately and discard only honours
Stop drawing tiles
Discard randomly to hide your shape
8-3.explanation: A player who needs points cannot profit from a draw, so taking risk to chase a larger hand is the correct trade.

8-4.question: You hold {{m2}}{{m3}}. Arrange its two winning tiles from lowest to highest.
8-4.explanation: A 23 shape is a two-sided wait, because both {{m1}} and {{m4}} complete the run.

8-4.question: You hold {{m4}}{{m6}}. How many different tile types complete this closed wait?
8-4.explanation: A closed wait has a hole in the middle, so only {{m5}} can fill it.

8-4.question: Which of these are two-sided waits?
options: {{m2}}{{m3}} waiting on {{m1}} or {{m4}}
{{p7}}{{p8}} waiting on {{p6}} or {{p9}}
{{s5}}{{s7}} waiting on {{s6}} only
{{m1}}{{m2}} waiting on {{m3}} only
8-4.explanation: A two-sided wait accepts two different tiles, so it has about twice as many winning tiles as a closed wait.

8-4.question: You want flexible waits. Which of these single tiles is the least useful to keep?
options: m1
m5
p5
s5
8-4.explanation: A terminal only fits one run, while a middle tile fits several, so terminals are the least flexible tiles to hold.

8-4.question: Which pair of tiles forms a closed wait (kanchan)?
8-4.explanation: The pair {{s5}}{{s7}} is one rank apart with a gap in the middle, which is the definition of a closed wait.

8-5.question: What does calling a Pong cost you?
options: It exposes part of your hand to opponents
It spends a turn you could have used to reshape your hand
It stops you from ever winning by self-draw
It forfeits the 1-Faan 門前清 bonus on an otherwise concealed hand
8-5.explanation: A call speeds the hand up but reveals tiles, reduces flexibility, and ends the concealed bonus.

8-5.question: Match each situation to the tempo choice that fits it.

pairs.left: One cheap meld away from a 3-Faan win, wall still deep
pairs.right: Call the meld and speed up

pairs.left: Promising 混一色 with plenty of tiles left
pairs.right: Stay concealed and build

pairs.left: Two opponents have called melds and the wall is thin
pairs.right: Slow down and defend

pairs.left: Far behind on points with few tiles left
pairs.right: Push for a big hand

8-5.explanation: Tempo should follow the table: speed up when a cheap win is near, slow down when others are faster or the wall is short.

8-5.question: An opponent calls Chow on their second turn. What is the main information this gives you?
options: Which suit they are collecting
Their exact winning tile
Nothing at all
Their current score
8-5.explanation: A Chow shows three tiles of one suit, which points to that suit without revealing the wait.

8-5.question: Staying concealed for the whole hand keeps 門前清, worth how many Faan?
8-5.explanation: 門前清 is a 1-Faan pattern, so any call that breaks concealment gives up exactly one Faan.

8-5.question: You are racing for the fastest possible win. Which of these single tiles is the least useful to hold?
options: east
m4
p5
s6
8-5.explanation: A lone honour needs two matching copies to become a meld, which is the slowest way to build a fast hand.

8-6.question: Turn 12. You are two tiles from ready and one opponent holds three melds. Which actions are correct?
options: Check what that opponent has discarded this rotation
Discard a fresh middle tile to keep your own shape
Break your hand to find a safe tile if no safe tile is free
Count how many copies of each candidate tile are already visible
8-6.explanation: Against a player who is close, safety comes first, so read their discards and visible copies rather than protecting shape.

8-6.question: Match each tactic to what it means.

pairs.left: Reading discards
pairs.right: Inferring a hand from what an opponent throws

pairs.left: Absolute safety
pairs.right: A tile the opponent discarded earlier this rotation

pairs.left: Folding
pairs.right: Discarding safe tiles instead of chasing your win

pairs.left: Tile efficiency
pairs.right: Maximising the tiles that complete your hand

8-6.explanation: These four ideas are the whole tactical toolkit: read the table, judge safety, know when to fold, and count your outs.

8-6.question: An opponent is one tile from winning. Arrange these discards from safest to most dangerous: {{red}}, which they threw earlier this rotation; {{p9}}, of which three copies are visible; {{s2}}, which nobody has played.
8-6.explanation: A tile they already discarded is safe this rotation, three visible copies leave only one live copy, and an unseen tile leaves all four.

8-6.question: Three copies of {{s8}} are visible on the table. How many copies can an opponent still be holding?
8-6.explanation: Four copies exist in total, so with three visible exactly one copy is still live and it may be in any hand or the wall.

8-6.question: Which single habit improves both your attack and your defence?
options: Watching every discard and counting visible copies
Calling the first meld offered every hand
Never discarding honour tiles
Always keeping one pair in hand
8-6.explanation: Discard reading and copy counting drive both your own wait choices and your safety judgements, so one habit serves both sides.
